Two light waves having the same wavelength $\lambda$ in vacuum are in phase initially. Then the first wave travels a path ${L}_{1}$ through a medium of refractive index ${n}_{1}$while the second wave travels a path of length ${L}_{2}$ through a medium of refractive index ${n}_{2}$. After this the phase difference between the two waves is:
questions.explanation:
The optical path between any two points is proportional to the time of travel.

The distance traversed by light in a medium of refractive index $\mu$ in time $t$ is given by $d = \mathrm{vt}$ .......(i)

Where $v$ is velocity of light in the medium. The distance traversed by light in a vacuum in this time,

$s = ct = c \times \frac{d}{v}$ [from equation (i)]

$= d\frac{c}{v} = \mathrm{μd}$ .....(ii) (Since$\mu = \frac{c}{v}$)

This distance is the equivalent distance in vacuum and is called optical path.

Here, optical path for first ray $= {n}_{1}{L}_{1}$

Optical path for second ray $= {n}_{2}{L}_{2}$

Path difference $= {n}_{1}{L}_{1} - {n}_{2}{L}_{2}$

Now, phase difference $= \frac{2\pi }{\lambda } \times$path difference

$= \frac{2\pi }{\lambda } \times \left({n}_{1}{L}_{1} - {n}_{2}{L}_{2}\right)$

questions.question: In a Young’s double slit experiment, two slits are illuminated with a light of wavelength $800\mathrm{nm}$. The line joining ${A}_{1}P$ is perpendicular to ${A}_{1}{A}_{2}$ as shown in the figure. If the first minimum is detected at $P$, the value of slits separation $a$ will be : The distance of screen from slits $D = 5\mathrm{cm}$.
questions.explanation: The position of first minima is $y = \frac{\lambda D}{2 \times a}$($y$ is height of the point from the axis passing through the mid-point of ${A}_{1}\text{and}{A}_{2}$) Since the first minima is in front of the slit as shown in the figure, $\frac{\lambda D}{2 \times a} = \frac{a}{2} \implies a = \sqrt{\lambda D} = \sqrt{800 \times {10}^{ - 9} \times 5 \times {10}^{ - 2}} = 2 \times {10}^{ - 4}m = 0.2\mathrm{mm}$ !

questions.question: In a Young's double slit experiment, the path difference, at a certain point on the screen, betwen two interfering waves is $\frac{1}{8}$ th of wavelength. The ratio of the intensity at this point to that at the centre of a bright fringe is close to:
questions.explanation:
Given, path difference, $\Delta x=\frac{\lambda}{8}$

Phase difference $(\Delta \phi)$ is given by

$\Delta \phi=\frac{2 \pi}{\lambda}(\Delta \mathrm{x}) \Delta \phi=\frac{(2 \pi)}{\lambda} \frac{\lambda}{8}=\frac{\pi}{4}$

For two sources in different phases,$$\begin{array}{l}

I=I_{0} \cos ^{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{8}\right) \\

\frac{1}{I_{0}}=\cos ^{2}\left(\frac{\pi}{8}\right) \\

=\frac{1+\cos \frac{\pi}{4}}{2}=\frac{1+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}}{2}=0.85

\end{array}$$ `

questions.question: The width of one of the two slits in a Young's double slit experiment is 4 times that of the other slit. The ratio of the maximum of the minimum intensity in the interference pattern is:
questions.explanation: Since, Intensity $\propto$ width of slit $(\omega) \begin{aligned} & \text { so, } I_1=I, I_2=4 \mathrm{I} \\ & I_{\min }=\left(\sqrt{I_1}-\sqrt{I_2}\right)^2=I \\ & I_{\max }=\left(\sqrt{I_1}+\sqrt{I_2}\right)^2=9 \mathrm{I} \\ & \frac{I_{\max }}{I_{\min }}=\frac{9 \mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{I}}=\frac{9}{1} \end{aligned}$ ;

questions.question: In a Young's double slit experiment, an angular width of the fringe is $0.35 ^\circ$ on a screen placed at $2m$ away for particular wavelength of $450\mathrm{nm}$. The angular width of the fringe, when whole system is immersed in a medium of refractive index $\frac{7}{5}$, is $\frac{1}{\alpha }$. The value of $\alpha$ is _____ .
questions.explanation:
Angular fringe width is given by $\theta = \frac{\lambda }{D}$, where, $D$ is the distance between the source and the screen and $\lambda$ is the wavelength of the light.

We have, $\frac{{\theta }_{1}}{{\theta }_{2}} = \frac{{\lambda }_{1}}{{\lambda }_{2}}$

Then, ${\theta }_{2} = \frac{{0.35}^{∘}}{450\mathrm{nm}} \times \frac{450\mathrm{nm}}{\frac{7}{5}} = {0.25}^{∘} = \frac{1}{4} \left(∵{\lambda }_{2} = \frac{{\lambda }_{1}}{\mu }\right)$

Thus, value of $\alpha = 4$.

questions.question: If the measured angular separation between the second minimum to the left of the central maximum and the third minimum to the right of the central maximum is $30^{\circ}$ in a single slit diffraction pattern recorded using 628 nm light, then the width of the slit is _______ $\mu \mathrm{m}$.
questions.explanation: $\begin{aligned} & \theta_1=\sin ^{-1}\left(\frac{2 \lambda}{a}\right) \\ & \theta_2=\sin ^{-1}\left(\frac{3 \lambda}{a}\right) \\ & \because \quad \theta_1+\theta_2=30^{\circ}\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow \sin ^{-1}\left(\frac{2 \lambda}{\mathrm{a}}\right)+\sin ^{-1}\left(\frac{3 \lambda}{\mathrm{a}}\right)=\frac{\pi}{6} \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{2 \lambda}{\mathrm{a}} \sqrt{1-\left(\frac{3 \lambda}{\mathrm{a}}\right)^2}+\frac{3 \lambda}{\mathrm{a}} \sqrt{1+\left(\frac{2 \lambda}{\mathrm{a}}\right)^2}=\sin \frac{\pi}{6}\end{aligned}$ Here $\lambda=628 \mathrm{~nm}$ After solving $\mathrm{A}=6.07 \mu \mathrm{~m}$ Approximate Method : $\begin{aligned} & \theta=\theta_1+\theta_2 \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{2 \lambda}{a}+\frac{3 \lambda}{a} \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{\pi}{6}=\frac{5}{a}(628 \mathrm{~nm}) \\ & \Rightarrow a=6 \mu \mathrm{~m}\end{aligned}$

questions.question: In a double slit experiment shown in figure, when light of wavelength $400\mathrm{nm}$ is used, dark fringe is observed at $P$. If $D = 0.2m$, the minimum distance between the slits ${S}_{1}$ and ${S}_{2}$ is $\alpha \mathrm{mm}$. Write the value of $10\alpha$ to the nearest integer.
questions.explanation: According to the given diagram, the path difference for minima at P is given by $\Delta x = 2\sqrt{{D}^{2} + {d}^{2}} - 2D...\left(1\right)$ And, from the condition of minima, it follows that $\Delta x = \frac{\lambda }{2}...\left(2\right)$ Equations (1) and (2) imply that $2\sqrt{{D}^{2} + {d}^{2}} - 2D = \frac{\lambda }{2} \implies \sqrt{{D}^{2} + {d}^{2}} - D = \frac{\lambda }{4} \implies \sqrt{{D}^{2} + {d}^{2}} = \frac{\lambda }{4} + D \implies {D}^{2} + {d}^{2} = {D}^{2} + \frac{{\lambda }^{2}}{16} + \frac{D\lambda }{2} \implies {d}^{2} = \frac{D\lambda }{2} + \frac{{\lambda }^{2}}{16} \implies {d}^{2} = \frac{0.2 \times 400 \times {10}^{ - 9}}{2} + \frac{16 \times {10}^{ - 14}}{16} \implies {d}^{2} \approx 400 \times {10}^{ - 10} \begin{matrix}∴d & = & 20 \times {10}^{ - 5}m \\ & = & 0.20\mathrm{mm}\end{matrix}$ Therefore, $10\alpha = 2$.

questions.question: In Young’s double slit experiment, two slits ${S}_{1}$ and ${S}_{2}$ are $d$ distance apart and the separation from slits to screen is $D$ (as shown in figure). Now if two transparent slabs of equal thickness $0.1\mathrm{mm}$ but refractive index $1.51$ and $1.55$ are introduced in the path of beam $\left(\lambda = 4000Å\right)$ from ${S}_{1}$ and ${S}_{2}$ respectively. The central bright fringe spot will shift by ________ number of fringes.
questions.explanation: The change in path difference due to the two slabs at $P$ is $\Delta x = \left({\mu }_{2} - {\mu }_{1}\right)t = (1.55 - 1.51) \times 0.1 = 0.04 \times {10}^{ - 4} \implies \Delta x = 4 \times {10}^{ - 6} = 4\mathrm{μm}$ Now, the distance of central maxima from geometrical center is $y = \frac{\Delta xD}{d} = 4 \times {10}^{ - 6}\frac{D}{d}$ Now, fringe width, $n\beta = 4 \times {10}^{ - 6}\frac{D}{d}$ Or, $\frac{n\lambda D}{d} = 4 \times {10}^{ - 6}\frac{D}{d}$ Number of shift, $n = \frac{4 \times {10}^{ - 6}}{4 \times {10}^{ - 7}} = 10$.

questions.question: As shown in the figure, in Young's double slit experiment, a thin plate of thickness $t = 10\mathrm{μm}$ and refractive index $\mu = 1.2$ is inserted infront of slit ${S}_{1}$. The experiment is conducted in air ($\mu = 1$) and uses a monochromatic light of wavelength $\lambda = 500\mathrm{nm}$. Due to the insertion of the plate, central maxima is shifted by a distance of $x{\beta }_{0}$. ${\beta }_{0}$ is the fringe-width before the insertion of the plate. The value of the $x$ is ______.
questions.explanation:
Fringe shift due to slab in Young's double slit experiment is given by $\Delta x = \frac{D(\mu - 1)t}{d}$

Since, fringe width ${\beta }_{0} = \frac{D}{d}\lambda$

Then, $\Delta x = \frac{{\beta }_{0}\left(\mu - 1\right)t}{\lambda }$

Putting the values, we have

$= \frac{10 \times {10}^{ - 6}(1.2 - 1)}{5 \times {10}^{ - 7}}{\beta }_{0} = \frac{{10}^{ - 5} \times 0.2}{5 \times {10}^{ - 7}}{\beta }_{0}\;$

Hence, the value of $x = 4$.

questions.question: In a Young’s double slit experiment, the intensities at two points, for the path difference $\frac{\lambda }{4}$ and $\frac{\lambda }{3}$ ($\lambda$ being the wavelength of light used) are ${I}_{1}$ and ${I}_{2}$ respectively. If ${I}_{0}$ denotes the intensity produced by each one of the individual slits, then $\frac{{I}_{1} + {I}_{2}}{{I}_{0}} = ______$.
questions.explanation:
As we know, resultant intensity is given by,

$I = 4{I}_{0}{\cos }^{2}\left(\frac{\Delta ϕ}{2}\right)$ and phase difference can be written as $\Delta ϕ = \frac{2\pi }{\lambda } \Delta x$.

For first case:

${I}_{1} = 4{I}_{0}{\cos }^{2}\left(\frac{2\pi }{\lambda } \times \frac{\lambda }{4}\right) = 4{I}_{0}{\cos }^{2}\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right) = 2{I}_{0}$

For second case:

${I}_{2} = 4{I}_{0}{\cos }^{2}\left(\frac{2\pi }{\lambda } \times \frac{\lambda }{3}\right) = 4{I}_{0}{\cos }^{2}\left(\frac{2\pi }{3}\right) = {I}_{0}$

Therefore, required value of$\frac{{I}_{1} + {I}_{2}}{{I}_{0}} = 3$.

questions.question: In a Young's double slit experiment, a laser light of $560\mathrm{nm}$ produces an interference pattern with consecutive bright fringes' separation of $7.2\mathrm{mm}$. Now another light is used to produce an interference pattern with consecutive bright fringes' separation of $8.1\mathrm{mm}$. The wavelength of second light is _____ $\mathrm{nm}.$
questions.explanation:
Given here: ${\lambda }_{1} = 560 \times {10}^{ - 9}m$, ${\beta }_{1} = 7.2 \times {10}^{ - 3}m$ and ${\beta }_{2} = 8.1 \times {10}^{ - 3}m$.

Let $d$ be the width and $D$ be the distance between slit and screen then fringe width, $\beta = \frac{\lambda D}{d}$.

Thus, from above, $\beta \propto \lambda$

So, the wavelength of second light is ${\lambda }_{2} = \frac{{\beta }_{2}}{{\beta }_{1}}{\lambda }_{1} = \frac{9}{8}{\lambda }_{1} ∴{\lambda }_{2} = \frac{9}{8} \times 560 = 630\mathrm{nm}.$

`

questions.question: The width of one of the two slits in a Young's double slit experiment is three times the other slit. If the amplitude of the light coming from a slit is proportional to the slit-width, the ratio of minimum to maximum intensity in the interference pattern is $x : 4$ where $x$ is $_______.$

Also intensity $\propto(\text { Amplitude })^2 \propto(\text { Slit width })^2 \frac{I_1}{I_2}=\left(\frac{3}{1}\right)^2=9 \Rightarrow I_1=9 I_2 \frac{I_{\min }}{I_{\max }}=\left(\frac{\sqrt{I_1}-\sqrt{I_2}}{\sqrt{I_1}+\sqrt{I_2}}\right)^2=\left(\frac{3-1}{3+1}\right)^2=\frac{1}{4}=\frac{x}{4} \Rightarrow x=1$ ,

questions.question: A double slit interference experiment performed with a light of wavelength 600 nm forms an interference fringe pattern on a screen with 10 th bright fringe having its centre at a distance of 10 mm from the central maximum. questions.question:
Given below are two statements :

Statement I : If the Brewster's angle for the light propagating from air to glass is ${\theta }_{B}$, then Brewster's angle for the light propagating from glass to air is $\frac{\pi }{2} - {\theta }_{B}$.

Statement II : The Brewster's angle for the light propagating from glass to air is ${\tan }^{ - 1}\left({\mu }_{g}\right)$, where ${\mu }_{g}$ is the refractive index of glass.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below :
options: Both Statements I and Statement II are true.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.
questions.explanation: Applying Snell's law, we get ${\mu }_{a}\sin i = {\mu }_{g}\sin \left(90 ^\circ - i\right) \tan i = \frac{{\mu }_{g}}{{\mu }_{a}}$ When going from glass to air $\tan {i}^{'} = \frac{{\mu }_{a}}{{\mu }_{g}} = \cot i$ Clearly, ${i}^{'} = \left(\frac{\pi }{2} - i\right)$ & hence Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.question: A microwave of wavelength $2.0\mathrm{cm}$ falls normally on a slit of width $4.0\mathrm{cm}.$ The angular spread of the central maxima of the diffraction pattern obtained on a screen $1.5m$ away from the slit, will be:

Therefore, angular spread of central maxima will be $= 2\theta = 60º$.

questions.question: The difference in the number of waves when yellow light propagates through air and vacuum columns of the same thickness is one. The thickness of the air column is _____ $\mathrm{mm}$. [Refractive index of air $= 1.0003$, the wavelength of yellow light in vacuum $= 6000\overset{∘}{A}]$

questions.question: Sodium light of wavelengths $650\mathrm{nm}$ and $655\mathrm{nm}$ is used to study diffraction at a single slit of aperture $0.5\mathrm{mm}$. The distance between the slit and the screen is $2.0m$. The separation between the positions of the first maxima of diffraction pattern obtained in the two cases is _____ $\times {10}^{ - 5}m$
questions.explanation:
The condition for maxima in diffraction is,

$b\sin \theta = \left(2n + 1\right)\frac{\lambda }{2}$.

For the first maxima $n = 1$. Therefore,

$b\sin \theta = \frac{3\lambda }{2}\;$

Now the difference between the positions of the maxima will be,

${y}_{1} - {y}_{2} = \frac{3D}{2b}\left({\lambda }_{1} - {\lambda }_{2}\right)\;$

questions.question: ‘$n$’ polarizing sheets are arranged such that each makes an angle $45 ^\circ$ with the proceeding sheet. An unpolarized light of intensity $I$ is incident into this arrangement. The output intensity is found to be $\frac{I}{64}$ . The value of $n$ will be:
questions.explanation:
When an unpolarized light passes through a polariser, the intensity of the emergent light from the polariser depends on the square of the cosine of the angle between the plane of the polariser and the direction of the incident light.

The formula to calculate the intensity $\left({I}_{1}\right)$ of the emergent light from a polariser which makes an angle $\theta$ with the direction of the incident light is given by

${I}_{1} = I{\cos }^{2}\theta ..................(1)$

where, $I$ is the intensity of the incident light.

Substitute $45 ^\circ$ for $\theta$ into equation (1) to obtain the intensity of the first emergent light.

$\begin{matrix}{I}_{1} & = & I{\cos }^{2}45 ^\circ \\ & = & \frac{I}{2}\end{matrix}$

In a similar manner, the intensity $\left({I}_{2}\right)$ of the second emergent light can be written as

$\begin{matrix}{I}_{2} & = & {I}_{1}{\cos }^{2}45 ^\circ \\ & = & \frac{{I}_{1}}{2} \\ & = & \frac{I}{4} \\ & = & \frac{I}{{2}^{2}}\end{matrix}$

Thus, for $n$ number of such polarisers, the net intensity $\left({I}_{n}\right)$ of the emergent light can be written as

${I}_{n} = \frac{I}{{2}^{n}}......................(1)$

Comparing equation (1) with the given expression for the intensity, it can be concluded that

$n = 6$

questions.question: As shown in figures, three identical polaroids ${P}_{1}$, ${P}_{2}$ and ${P}_{3}$ are placed one after another. The pass axis of ${P}_{2}$ and ${P}_{3}$ are inclined at angle of $60º$ and $90º$ with respect to axis of ${P}_{1}$. The source $S$ has an intensity of $256W{m}^{ - 2}$. questions.explanation:
As given here, the pass axis of ${P}_{2}$ and ${P}_{3}$ are inclined at angle of $60º$ and $90º$ with respect to axis of ${P}_{1}$.

Therefore, intensity of light after falling on first polaroid ${P}_{1},{I}_{1} = \frac{{I}_{0}}{2}$

Intensity of light after falling on second polaroid ${P}_{2},{I}_{2} = {I}_{1}{\cos }^{2}60 ^\circ = \frac{{I}_{0}}{8}$

The intensity of light at $O$ is $\frac{3{I}_{0}}{32} = \frac{3 \times 256}{32} = 24W{m}^{ - 2}$

questions.question: A system of three polarizers ${P}_{1},{P}_{2},{P}_{3}$ is set up such that the pass axis of ${P}_{3}$ is crossed with respect to that of ${P}_{1}$ . The ratio $\left({I}_{o} / I\right)$ equals (nearly):
questions.explanation: The intensity of light coming out of 1st Polaroid will be ${I}_{1} = \frac{{I}_{0}}{2}$ From Malus law $I = {I}_{0}{\cos }^{2}⁡\theta$ From Polaroid 2: $I = \frac{{I}_{0}}{2}{\cos }^{2}⁡30 ^\circ = \frac{{I}_{0}}{2}{\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)}^{2} = \frac{3{I}_{0}}{8}$ From Polaroid 3: $I = \frac{3{I}_{0}}{8}{\cos }^{2}⁡60 ^\circ = \frac{3{I}_{0}}{8}{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}^{2} = \frac{3{I}_{0}}{32}$ Now, $\frac{{I}_{0}}{I} = \frac{32}{3} = 10.67$

questions.question: When a polaroid sheet is rotated between two crossed polaroids then the transmitted light intensity will be maximum for a rotation of :
questions.explanation:
Let ${I}_{0}$ be intensity of unpolarised light incident on first polaroid.

${I}_{1} =$ Intensity of light transmitted from ${1}^{\text{st }}$ polaroid

$= \frac{{I}_{0}}{2}$

If $\theta$ be the angle between ${1}^{\text{st }}$ and ${2}^{\text{nd }}$ polaroid and $ϕ$ be the angle between ${2}^{\text{nd }}$ and ${3}^{\text{rd }}$ polaroid, then

$\theta + ϕ = 90 ^\circ ...\left(1\right)$

If ${I}_{2} =$ Intensity from ${2}^{\text{nd }}$ polaroid,

$\begin{matrix}{I}_{2} & = & {I}_{1}co{s}^{2}\theta \\ & = & \frac{{I}_{0}}{2}co{s}^{2}\theta \end{matrix}$

If ${I}_{3} =$ Intensity from ${3}^{\text{rd }}$ polaroid

$\begin{matrix}{I}_{3} & = & {I}_{2}co{s}^{2}ϕ \\ & = & {I}_{1}{\cos }^{2}\theta {\cos }^{2}ϕ \\ & = & \frac{{I}_{0}}{2}co{s}^{2}\theta co{s}^{2}\left(90 ^\circ - \theta \right) \\ & = & \frac{{I}_{0}}{2}co{s}^{2}\theta si{n}^{2}\theta \\ & = & \frac{{I}_{0}}{2}{\left(\frac{2\sin \theta \cos \theta }{2}\right)}^{2} \\ & = & \frac{{I}_{0}}{8}{\sin }^{2}2\theta \end{matrix}$

Now, ${I}_{3}$ will be maximum when

$\sin 2\theta = 1 \implies 2\theta = 90 ^\circ \implies \theta = 45 ^\circ$

questions.question: A beam of plane polarized light of large cross-sectional area and uniform intensity of $3.3W{m}^{–2}$ falls normally on a polarizer (cross-sectional area $3 \times {10}^{–4}{m}^{2}$), which rotates about its axis with an angular speed of $31.4\mathrm{rad}{s}^{ - 1}$. The energy of light passing through the polarizer per revolution, is close to:
questions.explanation: Given, Intensity of plane polarized light of large cross-sectional area is ${I}_{0} = 3.3W{m}^{ - 2}$ Area of cross-section of polarizer is $A = 3 \times {10}^{ - 4}{m}^{2}$ Angular speed of rotation is $\omega = 31.4\mathrm{rad}{s}^{ - 1}$ The intensity of light is the given by the definition, $I = \frac{E}{AT}...(1)$ Intensity of light passing through the polarizer as polarizer rotates is given by ${I}_{avg} = {I}_{0}\frac{1}{T}{ \int }_{0}^{T}{\cos }^{2}\left(\omega t\right)dt \implies {I}_{avg} = {I}_{0}\frac{1}{T}{ \int }_{0}^{T}\left(\frac{1 + \cos \left(2\omega t\right)}{2}\right)dt \implies {I}_{avg} = {I}_{0}\frac{1}{2T}\left({ \int }_{0}^{T}dt + { \int }_{0}^{T}\cos \left(2\omega t\right)dt\right) \implies {I}_{avg} = {I}_{0}\frac{1}{2T}\left(T + 0\right) \implies {I}_{avg} = \frac{{I}_{0}}{2}...(2)$ Using equation (1) and (2) we get energy per revolution is given by $E = \frac{{I}_{0}A}{2}T = \frac{{I}_{0}A}{2}\frac{2\pi }{\omega } E = \frac{3.3 \times 3 \times {10}^{−4}}{2}\frac{3.14}{31.4} E≃1 \times {10}^{ - 4}J$ !

questions.question:
Unpolarised light is incident on the boundary between two dielectric media, whose dielectric constants are $2.8$ (medium –$1$) and $6.8$ (medium – $2$), respectively. To satisfy the condition, so that the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular to each other, the angle of incidence should be ${\tan }^{ - 1}{\left(1 + \frac{10}{\theta }\right)}^{\frac{1}{2}}$, the value of $\theta$ is ______.

(Given for dielectric media, ${\mu }_{r} = 1$)
questions.explanation:
As given in the question, we can write

${\mu }_{1} = \sqrt{{\epsilon }_{r}{\mu }_{r}} = \sqrt{2.8 \times 1} = \sqrt{2.8}$ and

${\mu }_{2} = \sqrt{{\epsilon }_{r}{\mu }_{r}} = \sqrt{6.8 \times 1} = \sqrt{6.8}$

Now applying Snell's law and considering $r = 90 ^\circ - i$, we get

${\mu }_{1}\sin i = {\mu }_{2}\cos i \implies \tan i = \frac{{\mu }_{2}}{{\mu }_{1}} = \sqrt{\frac{6.8}{2.8}} \implies \tan i = {\left(\frac{2.8 + 4}{2.8}\right)}^{\frac{1}{2}} \implies i = {\tan }^{ - 1}{\left(1 + \frac{10}{7}\right)}^{\frac{1}{2}}$

Therefore, $\theta = 7$.
